Article Title: PM Modi: I forgive those who abused me & my mother, our job to guide them
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Mistakes happen at a young age, says PM Modi

NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi said on Friday he will forgive young protesters accused of abusing him and his late mother, saying they are misguided children and it is “our job to show them the right way”.In a video message, Modi said punishing these youth and making them run around courts will not change circumstances, adding that these children have lost their way and must be guided instead of being subjected to any harassment. His comments came amid incidents of criminal cases being lodged against some young protesters for abusing him during the recent student protest. “Everybody saw what happened at Jantar Mantar,” the PM said.They abused not only me but also my late mother. It was such a vile thing. But I want to say today that mistakes happen at a young age, and this is also the opportunity to correct those mistakes,” he said. “I want to forgive them. Society should also accept my decision,” he said in a clear indication that cases against these youngsters will be withdrawn. Modi as Gujarat CM had forgiven a youngster accused of sending a threatening mail to him, sources said.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi said on Friday he will forgive young protesters accused of abusing him and his late mother. He said punishing these youth and making them run around courts will not change circumstances. His comments came amid incidents of criminal cases being lodged against some young protesters for abusing him.

Article Title: The price of mockery
Article Text: Thirukkural with the Times explores real-world lessons from the classic Tamil text ‘Thirukkural’. Written by Tamil poet and philosopher Thiruvalluvar, the Kural consists of 1,330 short couplets of seven words each. This text is divided into three books with teachings on virtue, wealth, and love and is considered one of the great works ever on ethics and morality. The Kural has influenced scholars and leaders across social, political, and philosophical spheres. Motivational speaker, author and diversity champion Bharathi Bhaskar explores the masterpiece. There is a kind of ignorance that is harmless. Then there is another kind that troubles me deeply. It ridicules what it has never cared to learn. History, scholarship, art, music, literature and sacrifice become material for cheap amusement. The ancient Greeks called such people the Philistines . Whatever the label, the damage they cause is real. A recent television programme left me with precisely this feeling. It was presented as a comedy. Four young adults sat chatting casually. One participant asked the others, "Do you know V O C? What did he pull?" One participant guessed he must have been a boatman and therefore pulled a boat. Another remarked, "I thought he pulled a saree, like how Duryodhana did." In the Mahabharata, it was Dushasana, not Duryodhana, who dragged Draupadi's saree. The studio laughed. But who was really being laughed at? Not V O Chidambaram Pillai. It was our own history. V O C, revered as Kappalottiya Tamilan , challenged the British shipping monopoly by founding the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company in 1906. When Indian merchants suffered under the colonial shipping monopoly, he dared to dream of Indian-owned ships to sail between Tuticorin and Colombo. He raised funds, purchased two ships and stood up to an empire. The British retaliated with brutal vengeance. Arrested on charges of sedition, he was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment. Inside the prison, this distinguished lawyer was yoked to an oil press, forced to perform labour meant for bullocks. Those agonising years earned him the title Sekkizhuththa Semmal . Poverty marked the rest of his life, but his sacrifice became a foundation for India's political and economic freedom. It was this extraordinary life that became a punchline. Ignorance is never a crime. Ridiculing greatness is. Psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger described this tendency in 1999. The Dunning-Kruger effect explains how people with very little knowledge often possess enormous confidence while failing to recognise genuine expertise. Perhaps that is why a classical musician, an accomplished dancer, a gifted artist, a poet, a scientist or a freedom fighter can become easy targets. Even in schools, children who excel in studies are sometimes mocked or bullied simply because they perform well. Such ridicule often grows from insecurity, resentment and the inability to appreciate another's excellence. Thiruvalluvar recognised this danger centuries ago. He devoted an entire chapter to Periyaarai Pizhaiyaamai . In Kural 896 , he says: Eriyaal Sudappadinum Uyvuundaam; Uyyaar Periyaarp Pizhaithozhu Vaar One may escape from flames, but none escape the consequences of insulting the great Valluvar 's wisdom does not stop with freedom fighters or celebrated personalities. It quietly crosses the threshold of our homes. How often do we see ageing parents or in-laws spoken to with impatience, mocked or dismissed as outdated? More painful still, how often do parents remain silent when their own children belittle grandparents? Respect for elders is not an old-fashioned custom. It is the moral foundation of every enduring culture. The day we begin laughing at those who carried us before we could walk, taught us before we could read and sacrificed before we could dream, we have diminished ourselves. A society that mocks its achievers, bullies its brightest children and humiliates its elders is not progressing. It has quietly vanquished its soul.
Article Summary: Bharathi Bhaskar explores real-world lessons from the classic Tamil text 'Thirukkural' Written by Tamil poet and philosopher Thiruvalluvar, the Kural consists of 1,330 short couplets of seven words each.

Article Title: Reaction teams to flag 'fake info' on E20 blending
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Learning from the recent student protests led by CJP, govt has set up a team of officials from multiple ministries to counter online “misinformation” on E20 fuel through coordinated efforts by different stakeholders, including vehicle manufacturers, dealers, vehicle testing agencies, oil marketing companies and fuel pump dealers. Ministries concerned are also setting up Quick Response Teams (QRTs) to flag fake content.TOI has learnt that the team of officials from different ministries, including I&B, road transport, heavy industries and petroleum, is working together to deal with both proliferation of wrong information and also to put across the details that are backed by scientific and research-based reports. It’s focusing both on the young generation who are more active on different social media platforms and the targeted age groups who own vehicles as well.People aware of the development said this was one such rare occasion when there is a “coordinated and concerted effort” by different departments to put forward govt’s views backed by facts and scientific proof rather than individual departments fighting their own battle. They added, besides countering claims and allegations, testimonies of users and assurances of both vehicle manufacturers and oil marketing companies are also being put on social media platforms for online viewers.Officials added that govt has attached greatest importance to counter the ongoing campaign against ethanol blending and demand for going back to E0 (pure petrol) amid different organisations and political parties trying to garner support from people.While Aam Aadmi Party chief Arvind Kejriwal is holding a townhall against E20 in the capital on Saturday, activist Tehseen Poonawalla has announced a silent march and hunger strike in Delhi.
Article Summary: Ministries concerned are also setting up Quick Response Teams (QRTs) to flag fake content. It’s focusing both on the young generation who are more active on different social media platforms and the targeted age groups who own vehicles as well.

Article Title: The new public life of bats
Article Text:
Rohit Chakravarty led a bat walk at Sunder Nursery on April 17 to mark International Bat Appreciation Day and launch Delhi-NCR's first bat field guide

Rajesh Puttaswamaiah founded Bat Conservation India Trust in 2014

Kolar Leaf-Nosed Bat by Rajesh Puttaswamaiah

Beyond viruses and villainy

When hobby became conservation

Rajkumar Patel, who leads guided walks through Mumbai's rock-cut Buddhist caves, explains bat echolation using ultrasound detectors

Nobody grows up wanting to be a bat person. Unless your parents fell in love over dead ones. For Aditya Srinivasulu, bats were never mysterious creatures of the night. They were family lore. Long before he became a bat biologist himself, the UK-trained researcher grew up with the now-famous story of how his parents — renowned zoologists at Osmania University, Chelmala and Bhargavi Srinivasulu — fell in love over dead bats. As college classmates, Bhargavi gifted Chelmala a dead bat instead of roses; years later, Chelmala returned the gesture with another dead bat on their wedding day. Fortunately, Aditya jokes, there is no pressure on him to replicate the romantic gesture. Today, when Aditya is not doing his academic heavy-lifting, he conducts evening bat walks across the sprawling green campus of Osmania University.The setting is a biodiverse, wooded stretch where evening descends over a shrinking summer lake and the sky begins to flicker with movement. "If you stand there and look up, the sky is littered with a swirling mass of bats," Aditya says. "Think of a swarm of mosquitoes over your head near a lake — that kind of density.Except these are bats." Most of the tiny, fluttering shapes overhead are pipistrelles, among the smallest bats in South Asia. Then there are the crowd favourites: the flying foxes. "Big leathery boys," Aditya calls them affectionately. These large fruit bats emerge in dramatic numbers at dusk, soaring overhead while participants stand along the bund walkway. Sometimes they come within ten feet of the group. "As long as people don't make sudden movements or do flash photography, there's no issue," he says. The myth-busting happens organically. Bats are not blind, not aggressive, not waiting to fly into human hair. Fruit bats actually possess excellent eyesight and an extraordinary sense of smell. Families, retirees, students and curious residents from across Hyderabad show up. "Honestly, the children are always the highlight," Aditya says. The team hands out tiny stuffed bat plushies, and he watches reluctant children transform from "my parents dragged me here" to suddenly being completely fascinated. "Children ask the smartest questions. One child once asked if bats use sound to figure out where they're going, how do they think so quickly?" Srinivasulu remembers pausing, momentarily stumped by the question. "Anything that goes bump in the night immediately gets associated with witchcraft, bad omens or danger. Animals like bats, owls and snakes are burdened by stigma and misinformation," says the 28-year-old scion of the OG bat family of Hyderabad; he is now developing booklets and brochures on the city's bat diversity aimed at everyone from four-year-olds to researchers.Aditya is not alone. Bat researchers across Indian cities are beginning to trade the lab coat for the headlamp, leading groups of curious oglers through darkening parks and ruins, passing around ultrasound detectors like prized telescopes to catch bat calls and translate them into a crackling chorus of clicks and static bursts. For most participants, it's the first time they've not just seen a bat, but actually heard one "think" with echolocation. These researchers will tell you bats are the unacknowledged night-shift workers. When birds clock out at dusk, bats take over pollinating flowers, scattering seeds and hoovering up the kinds of insects that would otherwise devastate crops. Yet for a country that hosts around 135 bat species — roughly 10 percent of the world's total — India has remarkably few people who actually study them. That imbalance is precisely why many researchers now say that getting the public on board matters as much as any fieldwork."One of the biggest challenges is the lack of data or public participation when it comes to bats. Scientists alone cannot monitor every colony or every park. But ordinary citizens can," says Nikhil John, a naturalist with WWF India's Nature Connect outreach programme. That idea drove WWF India's recent bat walks in Delhi, organised around International Bat Appreciation Day in April, which also marked the launch of a first-of-its-kind fold-out guide to the bats of Delhi-NCR. It documents 12 of the 15 species recorded in the region, complete with identification tips, habitats and where people might actually spot them across the city. The first walk at Sunder Nursery last month drew around 65 people. A second walk to Tughlaqabad Fort the next day merged natural history with architecture and storytelling.While birds have long dominated India's citizen-science culture, bats have mostly remained invisible. There are birders everywhere. WhatsApp groups swap photographs from dawn trails, hobbyists upload sightings onto eBird, entire communities are built around identifying warblers and raptors. Bats instead are heard but not recorded, feared more than followed, thanks to haunted house and vampire movie mythologies. Conversationalists hope these walks become the springboard for a broader base of bat-watchers. John compares it to the rise of dragonfly festivals which transformed a largely ignored insect into a community-led conservation movement. "We now have volunteers and young people who are not from biodiversity or zoological backgrounds, but they can now talk about dragonflies and conduct walks." The hope is to replicate that energy for bats. "This year we are also trying to do a three-day Bat Festival in Delhi," John says.Back in the pandemic era, when early evidence linked bats to the SARS-CoV-2 virus, they became global villains overnight. Alarming viral spillover theories prompted a wave of widespread—and often misguided—public fear, with calls for culling and roost destruction. And suddenly, bats needed a PR team. “With the unnecessary villainization of bats, we had to step up and be more vocal online in those days,” says Rohit Chakravarty, who has become one of the most visible public voices for bat conservation in India. The 34-year-old speaks at lit fests and schools, gives lectures in bars and cafés through Bengaluru’s 'Pint of View series, and leads twilight bat walks through lakes, gardens and medieval ruins in Delhi and Bengaluru. He is also one of the editors of a hefty, 200-page 'State of India's Bats (2024–2025)' report, the first-ever national assessment of bat species in India, compiled by 36 experts from 27 institutions, released by the Nature Conservation Foundation (NCF) and Bat Conservation International (BCI) in collaboration with WWF India . Although released last month, the report's genesis really was the pandemic years, when researchers across India began collaborating on public statements against the killing of bats. "I think the Covid-era was a great turning point because we managed to convert the crisis into a more positive outcome," says Chakravarty. One of the report's central concerns is bats living in monuments. In Delhi, many protected monuments still shelter bat colonies because cities have lost most natural roosting spaces, yet bats are often treated as pests during restoration work. "This has been a cause of friction between the ASI and bat researchers for a long time. We're trying to understand why bats are disliked in these spaces, how we can conserve them in monuments when there are no natural roosts left around cities, and how these spaces can become opportunities for public awareness," he says. But he is careful not to romanticise bats as harmless mascots. "Any wild animal is dangerous. If you are in the same room with a tiger, the tiger will eat you. But if you are in the same room with a bat, the bat will not kill and eat you but the risk of disease is there from any wild animal." During enclosed monument walks, participants wear masks and maintain distance from roosting colonies. "Let's not single out bats. This applies to every animal."Rajkumar Patel, another researcher who leads guided bat walks through Mumbai's ancient rock-cut Buddhist caves at Mahakali in Jogeshwari and Kanheri inside Sanjay Gandhi National Park, gets particularly irritated about bat-blaming when it comes to zoonotic viruses from Covid to Nipah. "Bats carry pathogens but spillover happens when viruses jump species barriers through habitat destruction, wildlife trade, unsanitary conditions in wet markets and contamination like uncovered toddy sap collection sites. People should be more scared of mosquitoes and pigeons. They're far more likely to transmit disease to you. How many times in your day do you actually come face-to-face with a bat?" Patel asks.His walks have participants hunting for clues in the dark: urine stains on cave ceilings, bat shit (guano) on stone floors, discarded insect wings and, if they're lucky, spotting insectivorous species like Schneider's leaf-nosed bat or the black-bearded tomb bat hanging upside down in the shadows. His favourite conversational detour is the false vampire bat, a carnivorous hunter that preys on amphibians, birds and even smaller bats. "False" only because the actual blood-drinkers live in the Americas. "But mosquitoes also suck blood. Leeches too. But as soon as we mention bats, people get really scared. That kind of partiality should be eliminated completely." He also translates bats into a language everyone understands:F&B. "Mahua flowers, central to local liquor economies in central India, depend on fruit bats for pollination. Bananas, too. Tequila, one of the most trending drinks today, owes its existence to bats who are the primary natural pollinators of the blue agave plant. You won't get chocolates too without bats. They act as natural pest controllers in cocoa plantations, eating insects that would otherwise damage cocoa pods."Not all of India's bat advocates came through the academic route. Some simply fell into it and never climbed back out. For Bengaluru-based Rajesh Puttaswamaiah, it started with a stack of forgotten film slides. A corporate lawyer and entrepreneur, he spent the 1990s as a birder and wildlife enthusiast before stumbling, while digitising old slides in 2011, upon bat photographs nobody around him could identify. "Wildlife conservationists back then would talk tiger, elephants, birds, leopards, but how come no one ever talked about bats? The existing public photos online didn't help either. These images showed bats stretched out with their wings in awkward positions. Not really attractive. There are already so many negative myths about bats, and when you show them in an ugly manner, it doesn't help." So he decided to fix both problems. First through better photography, then by founding the Bat Conservation India Trust in 2014. Today his focus is the critically endangered Kolar leaf-nosed bat, rediscovered in 2013 near Hanumanahalli village in Karnataka's Kolar district by a team led by Bhargavi Srinivasulu, one of the few female bat researchers in India. The bat exists nowhere else on earth. When Puttaswamaiah arrived in 2019, the mood was hostile: quarrying on the granite hillock housing the bats had just been stopped and locals were furious. "They used to come and shout at us, saying, 'Because of you people, we lost our livelihood.'" Slowly, trust followed. "We tried to instil a sense of pride in them by saying that this is a rare bat found nowhere else in the world except their village," he says. Hunting dropped, children stopped disturbing roosts, farmers cut back on pesticides and locals were persuaded to protect the tamarind and Pongamia trees the bats feed on. It has since grown into a 10-year management action plan with the forest department.But not every conservation story soars. An attempt to work with the Bomrr clan in Nagaland — who traditionally hunted bats — had to be abandoned after running into financial and cultural barriers. Members of the Bomrr clan in Nagaland traditionally hunt fulvous fruit bat colonies every year after the monsoon."They sometimes smoke out entire caves, killing not just fulvous fruit bats but also other cave-dwelling species," says Puttaswamaiah. He says his team spent two years and a lot of money trying to negotiate a compromise. "But they were not inclined toward that. For them, it is an annual ritual, and their belief was that unless they hunted and ate these bats, their ancestors would not accept them. So ultimately, the project had to be shelved," he says. "Without involving local communities, we can't do any conservation," says Puttaswamaiah. Bat conservation, he has learned, is as much about navigating culture, livelihoods and identity as it is about science.
Article Summary: International Bat Appreciation Day marked around the world on April 17. Researchers across Indian cities are beginning to trade the lab coat for the headlamp. Bats are not blind, not aggressive, not waiting to fly into human hair. Fruit bats actually possess excellent eyesight and an extraordinary sense of smell.

Article Title: Wife of international kabaddi player Sheelu Balhara dies by suicide
Article Text:
Muskan Balhara, wife of international kabaddi player Sheelu Balhara, allegedly died by suicide (Image Credit:X)





ROHTAK: Muskan Balhara, wife of international kabaddi player Sheelu Balhara, allegedly died by suicide at her residence in Bahu Akbarpur village of Rohtak district on Friday evening.Rohtak SP Gaurav Rajpurohit said an investigation is underway and family members’ statements are being recorded. Balhara was being questioned as well but no official statement had been issued till late Friday night.Muskan’s family members staged a protest outside the house, alleging she was being harassed. A forensic team has inspected the house and collected evidence. Muskan’s body was taken to PGIMS-Rohtak.Muskan, who was from Farmana village in Meham, married Sheelu in Dec 2023. The couple has a nine-month-old son. Sheelu initially trained in judo and wrestling before taking up kabaddi at the age of six.Known as ‘Haryana Aala Cheeta’ in Punjab, Sheelu is a ‘catcher’ and has represented teams in India and abroad.
Article Summary: Muskan Balhara allegedly died by suicide at her residence in Bahu Akbarpur village of Rohtak district. An investigation is underway and family members’ statements are being recorded. Sheelu initially trained in judo and wrestling before taking up kabaddi at the age of six.

Article Title: Why Neeraj Chopra's CWG 2026 silver meant more with Yashvir Singh by his side in Glasgow
Article Text:
Neeraj Chopra (Image credit: Agencies)

Neeraj Chopra's medal record

'It feels great to be on the podium together'



Yashvir shines on Commonwealth Games debut



Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Neeraj Chopra added another medal to his glittering career at the Commonwealth Games, but the silver medal was not the only reason for his smile. The Olympic champion said sharing the podium with fellow Indian Yashvir Singh made the moment even more special.Neeraj finished second in the men's javelin throw with a season-best effort of 85.83m, while Commonwealth Games debutant Yashvir Singh clinched the bronze medal with a personal best throw of 85.41m in his final attempt. Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage claimed the gold with a best throw of 89.75m.Competing in only his second event of the season, Neeraj battled difficult weather conditions to throw 85.83m in his second attempt. The effort, his season best, was enough to earn him the silver medal in his second Commonwealth Games appearance. He had won the gold medal at the 2018 Commonwealth Games in Gold Coast.The CWG 2026 silver added to an already impressive medal collection that includes Olympic gold and silver, World Championships gold and silver, two Asian Games gold medals, a Commonwealth Games gold and silver, the Diamond League title, the Asian Championships gold, the South Asian Games gold and the U20 World Championships gold.Neeraj was full of praise for Yashvir, who produced the best throw of his career under pressure, and said sharing the podium with another Indian reminded him of the Asian Games medal double."It brings back memories of the Asian Games, where Saurav and I both won medals. I'm really happy that Yashvir achieved a personal best at such a crucial moment. It feels great to be on the podium together. It's always a joy to hear the national anthem play. That said, I also achieved a season-best, and my comeback is progressing well. There are more competitions ahead, so I'm very happy," Chopra told reporters.Yashvir emerged as the surprise package of the competition. The 24-year-old produced a personal best throw of 85.41m on his sixth and final attempt to win the bronze medal on his Commonwealth Games debut.He improved his previous personal best of 83.72m and finished ahead of several established names, including Anderson Peters and Arshad Nadeem.Reflecting on his medal-winning throw, Yashvir said he kept believing he could produce something special despite a slow start."This is my first international medal, and I am overjoyed. Everyone supported me, my family, my parents, everyone... I am truly happy about this... things were going a bit sluggishly at the start. At one point, my throw was around 81.3 meters. I saw that the bronze medal mark was sitting at 82 meters. I told myself, 'I've already thrown 82 meters--my personal best--in this competition, so I can definitely go beyond that. ' Things weren't going well up to the fifth throw, so for the final attempt, I decided to just go for it and see what happens. That last throw turned out really well," Singh said.
Article Summary: Neeraj Chopra won silver in the men's javelin throw at the Commonwealth Games. The Olympic champion threw 85.83m, his season-best effort. Fellow Indian Yashvir Singh won the bronze medal with a personal best of 85.41m. Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage claimed the gold with a best throw of 89.75m.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Seven months after her father's death, 23-year-old Tripura judoka Asmita Dey wins India's first Commonwealth Games judo gold
Article Text:
Asmita Dey (Image credit: Agencies)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Asmita Dey's historic Commonwealth Games gold medal was more than just India's first-ever top finish in judo. It was the fulfilment of a dream she once feared had ended with the death of her father seven months ago. The 23-year-old from a small village in Tripura scripted history by becoming the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal after defeating Canada's Heidi Quach in a dramatic women's 48kg final.After the win, emotions took over as Asmita remembered the man who had always believed in her."When my father passed away, I thought everything had finished because he was the one who supported me," Asmita said, struggling to hold back tears after her historic triumph.Asmita conceded an early yuko and also received a penalty, allowing Quach to take control. But the Indian judoka fought back, levelled the contest and kept her composure in the Golden Score period, where she landed the decisive yuko to seal a famous victory.After winning the gold medal, Asmita said her father always encouraged her to dream beyond the limits of their small village."I am from a very small village in Tripura. People there don't dream this big.But Papa always supported me," she said.Asmita recalled how her father stood by her."Mere papa hamesha mujhe support karte the. Beech mein mujhe injury hui thi, tab papa mere liye Delhi aaye the. Dawai, ilaaj, sab kuch unhone hi sambhala tha. Mummy-papa dono bahut support karte the, lekin mummy ko zyada samay nahi milta tha. Phir achanak 15 December ko papa ki death ho gayi. Uske baad laga ki sab kuch khatam ho gaya. Mujhe laga ki main kuch nahi kar paungi," she said."Papa jaane se pehle keh gaye the ki tum apne sapne ko aage badhana. Tum SAI Bhopal chale jao. Wahan SAI Bhopal mein mujhe bahut support mila. Thank you so much sir, kyunki main usi support ki wajah se aage badhi," Asmita said.
Article Summary: Asmita Dey is the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal. The 23-year-old defeated Canada's Heidi Quach in a dramatic women's 48kg final. Asmita said her father always encouraged her to dream beyond the limits of their small village.

Article Title: Injured Tejaswin Shankar scripts history; becomes first Indian to win decathlon medal in Commonwealth Games
Article Text:
India's Tejaswin Shankar competes in the men's decathlon 110m hurdles at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, Friday, July 31, 2026. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Tejaswin Shankar became the first Indian to win a Commonwealth Games medal in the men's decathlon after battling a long-standing knee injury to claim bronze in Glasgow on Friday.The national record holder finished with a total of 7,976 points in the 10-event competition, which is held over two days. He competed despite dealing with chronic patellar tendinitis, also known as jumper's knee, an injury that had forced him to withdraw from the men's high jump event earlier in the Games.The 27-year-old was left emotional after having to pull out of the high jump following his opening attempt because of the injury flare-up.This was Tejaswin's second Commonwealth Games medal after winning bronze in the men's high jump at the 2022 Birmingham Games. His national record in the decathlon stands at 8,057 points.Tejaswin, who also won silver in the decathlon at the 2023 Hangzhou Asian Games, ended the opening day in second place after five events, behind Canada's Damian Warner.He moved into third after the ninth event, the javelin throw, and held on to that position after finishing fifth in the 1,500m, the final event of the competition.Grenada's Lindon Victor, the Paris Olympics bronze medallist, won the gold with 8,096 points, while Warner took the silver with 8,036 points."I don't know if it was adversity or not. But I do know that the competitiveness in me is alive, and in these conditions and environment, I got the kick and the competitiveness," he said, as quoted by news agency PTI."I feel good to be in that position where I want to chase something but it is not guaranteed (to get success or not). I feel I am an adrenalin junkie ... I was enjoying the challenge, when I was standing for the 1500m (the last of the 10 events).""I will try to get that feeling back, get fitter and healthier and go and try to win gold in the Asian Games."
Article Summary: Tejaswin Shankar becomes first Indian to win a Commonwealth Games medal. The 27-year-old claims bronze in the men's decathlon in Glasgow. Shankar finished with a total of 7,976 points in the 10-event competition. He competed despite dealing with chronic patellar tendinitis.

Article Title: Gianni Infantino drops FIFA World Cup private equity plan after global backlash
Article Text:
Gianni Infantino (PTI Photo)

What was Infantino's proposal?



UEFA leads the opposition



Pressure grows on Infantino



Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Senior FIFA officials speak out



FIFA president Gianni Infantino has withdrawn his proposal to sell a stake in the commercial rights of the FIFA World Cup after facing widespread opposition from football bodies across the world.The decision came after several major football organisations, including UEFA, CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation, opposed the proposal. FIFA also saw senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro resign, while chief operating officer Kevin Lamour publicly criticised the plan.Announcing the decision on Friday, Infantino admitted the proposal had become too divisive."Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place. Our purpose has always been - and will always be - to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed."Infantino wanted to create a $20 billion company to manage FIFA's commercial business, including the men's and women's World Cups and Club World Cups. Under the proposal, private investors would own a 20% stake in the new company.The proposed "anchor investor" was a New York-based investment firm founded by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of U.S.President Donald Trump.The proposal triggered strong criticism from football's governing bodies. UEFA's 55 member associations even agreed to boycott FIFA competitions if the plan moved ahead.Explaining its stand, UEFA said: "Some things are simply too important to sell. The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale."CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation also announced their opposition to the proposal.The failed proposal has become one of the biggest setbacks of Infantino's presidency. Although he was re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023 and is eligible to seek one final four-year term under FIFA statutes, the controversy has raised fresh questions about his leadership.The next FIFA presidential election is scheduled to take place in Rabat, Morocco, with the deadline for candidates set for November 18, exactly four months before the vote.The controversy also reached FIFA's top leadership.Senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro resigned from his role after FIFA insisted: "Nobody is selling football."Cordeiro, however, made his position clear. "I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup."Soon after, FIFA chief operating officer Kevin Lamour criticised the proposal, saying many FIFA staff members had not been properly informed."It is the project of one person. Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."
Article Summary: FIFA president Gianni Infantino has withdrawn his proposal to sell a stake in the commercial rights of the FIFA World Cup. UEFA, CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation opposed the proposal. FIFA also saw senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro resign, while chief operating officer Kevin Lamour publicly criticised the plan.

Article Title: 'One day he could captain India': Selectors explain why 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi was named East Zone vice-captain
Article Text:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (ANI Photo)

The East Zone selectors have defended their decision to appoint 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi as vice-captain for the upcoming Duleep Trophy, describing the move as part of a long-term leadership plan rather than an indication of the team's pecking order.While Ishan Kishan 's appointment as captain was widely expected, the decision to hand the vice-captaincy to Sooryavanshi drew attention, especially with experienced campaigners such as Abhimanyu Easwaran Mohammed Shami and Mukesh Kumar also part of the squad.Sooryavanshi has featured in only eight first-class matches for Bihar, while Easwaran has played 113 first-class games and previously captained Bengal, India A and other representative sides.Explaining the reasoning behind the decision, Manish Vardhan, Jharkhand's representative on the East Zone selection committee, said the move was aimed at helping the youngster understand leadership from close quarters."We are not thinking about the present alone," Vardhan told Cricinfo. "A vice-captain gets to observe the captain closely and understand how a team is run. We wanted Vaibhav to be more involved with the group because we think it will help him as he develops."He's an extremely talented cricketer and is maturing steadily. Giving him this responsibility is another part of that process."Vardhan also clarified that Sooryavanshi's appointment does not automatically make him the stand-in captain if Kishan is unavailable.Although the selectors have not discussed that possibility, he suggested that an experienced player would likely take charge while Sooryavanshi continued as vice-captain.According to Vardhan, the committee's thinking behind appointing Kishan as captain was also based on long-term planning, with both Kishan and Sooryavanshi viewed as players capable of remaining in India's setup for many years."The vice-captain's role isn't about status," Vardhan said. "It's about what a young player can learn while working alongside the captain."Former Odisha cricketer and current selector-coach Pravanjan Mullick echoed those views, pointing out that Sooryavanshi has already served as Bihar's vice-captain in first-class cricket."Ishan is the captain and, as wicketkeeper, he is involved in every phase of the game," Mullick told Cricinfo. "This gives Vaibhav an opportunity to understand leadership without putting the responsibility of captaining the side on him. We want him to grow, maybe one day he could even captain India. That's the thought behind giving him the vice-captaincy."Cricinfo also reported that Easwaran was intentionally not considered for the vice-captain's role. The selection committee reportedly felt it would not be appropriate for the vastly experienced batter to serve as deputy to the comparatively inexperienced Kishan.
Article Summary: The East Zone selectors have defended their decision to appoint 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi as vice-captain for the upcoming Duleep Trophy. Manish Vardhan, Jharkhand's representative on the East Zone selection committee, said the move was aimed at helping the youngster understand leadership from close quarters. Article Title: Why Tom Brady still “hates” the 49ers despite becoming the GOAT
Article Text:
Why Tom Brady still “hates” the 49ers 25 years after they passed on him six times

The grudge Tom Brady refuses to retire: why he still "hates" the 49ers

Twenty-five years, seven rings, and he still isn't over it

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Tom Brady has seven Super Bowl rings, the most passing yards in NFL history, and absolutely nothing left to prove. And yet, 25 years later, there's still one wound that hasn't closed: the San Francisco 49ers, his hometown team, the team he grew up loving, passed on him six separate times in the 2000 NFL Draft. He has never let it go. He's not sure he ever will.Before he was the GOAT, Brady was just a Bay Area kid who idolized Joe Montana and grew up watching the 49ers dominate football in the 1980s and 90s. He was there, in some form, for the glory years, four Super Bowls, Bill Walsh's West Coast offense, Montana finding Dwight Clark for "The Catch." The 49ers weren't just a team to Brady. They were the standard.So when San Mateo's own local kid, a promising quarterback out of Michigan, entered the 2000 draft, it seemed almost written that San Francisco would call his name. They didn't. Not once, not twice, six times the 49ers took other players before finally, in the third round, settling on a different quarterback altogether: Hofstra's Giovanni Carmazzi. Brady would sit through the rest of that draft, watching team after team pass on him too, until New England scooped him up dead last in the sixth round, pick 199. The Patriots, for the record, had also passed on him five times before that, "just one less than everybody else," as Brady likes to point out.What happened next barely needs repeating: Brady became the most decorated quarterback in NFL history, while Carmazzi never played a single regular-season snap for San Francisco before retiring and, fittingly, becoming a goat farmer.It's a real-life football fable, and Brady has never resisted the urge to tell it. Every time he faced the 49ers over his 23-year career, he says, some part of him wanted to remind the men who'd been in that draft room exactly what they'd given up. "You chose a goat farmer over me," he's said, "and I never forgot that."He's repeated versions of the story for years on podcasts, in broadcast booths, in interviews timed to games against San Francisco, and each retelling carries the same mix of humor and genuine sting. He's admitted the 49ers even circled back years later, first reportedly considering him over Jimmy Garoppolo in 2020, then again in 2023 when Kyle Shanahan pursued him amid uncertainty over Brock Purdy's health. Both times, Brady said no. Whatever the reasons, it's hard not to read those refusals as their own quiet punctuation on the story Brady, for all his talk of love for the franchise, was never going back.Steve Mariucci, the 49ers' head coach at the time of the snub, has taken the ribbing in stride, noting that literally every team passed on Brady multiple times that year, and that he still loves the guy. Brady, for his part, seems to genuinely hold two things at once: real affection for the uniform he grew up watching, and real resentment toward the organization that decided, six separate times, that he wasn't good enough.He still watches their games. He still, by his own admission, can't bring himself to root for them.Twenty-five years and seven championships later, it's clear the chip on Brady's shoulder never really came off; he just found somewhere else to carry it.
Article Summary: The San Francisco 49ers passed on Tom Brady six separate times in the 2000 NFL Draft. Brady has never let it go, and he's not sure he ever will. He still watches their games, and still can't bring himself to root for them.

NEW DELHI: With more than a year left for the 2027 ODI World Cup, former India spinner Ravichandran Ashwin has shared the players he believes should be in the squad for the tournament.Speaking on ESPNcricinfo's YouTube channel, Ashwin divided the players into three categories - 'Yes', 'Maybe' and 'No' - while naming the cricketers he feels should be considered for the World Cup, which will be co-hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia from October 4 to November 21, 2027.One of Ashwin's biggest talking points was the inclusion of veteran pacer Bhuvneshwar Kumar , while players such as Rishabh Pant , Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Abhishek Sharma and Sanju Samson did not make his preferred squad.: Shubman Gill , Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Shreyas Iyer, KL Rahul, Ishan Kishan, Hardik Pandya , Axar Patel, Kuldeep Yadav, Jasprit Bumrah, Mohammed Siraj, Harshit Rana, Bhuvneshwar Kumar.: Yashasvi Jaiswal, Ruturaj Gaikwad, Varun Chakravarthy, Ravindra Jadeja, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Mohammed Shami, Arshdeep Singh, Prasidh Krishna.: Rishabh Pant, Washington Sundar, Sanju Samson, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Abhishek Sharma, Ravi Bishnoi, Shivam Dube, Prince Yadav, Gurnoor Brar.Ashwin believes Bhuvneshwar can still play an important role in South African conditions and said he should be given regular game time before the World Cup."Bhuvneshwar Kumar is a yes. Article Text:

India wicketkeeper-batter Rishabh Pant has started gearing up for the upcoming two-match Test series against Sri Lanka, with his preparations including a training session alongside former India captain MS Dhoni in Ranchi.A picture shared by former India spinner Shahbaz Nadeem from a gym in Ranchi showed Pant and Dhoni training together. While Dhoni was dressed in a blue tracksuit, Pant wore a black T-shirt and shorts.Sharing the photo on social media, Nadeem wrote, "Two of the best finishers of indian cricket @rishabpant and @mahi7781 bhai."Although Pant is currently out of India's white-ball setup, he continues to be a key member of the Test squad led by Shubman Gill .The 28-year-old heads into the Sri Lanka series after a disappointing IPL 2026 season with Lucknow Super Giants. Leading the franchise, Pant scored 312 runs in the tournament at an average of 28.36 and a strike rate of 138.05 as LSG finished at the bottom of the points table.Pant was last seen in competitive action during India's one-off Test against Afghanistan in Mullanpur in June.India have little margin for error in the ongoing World Test Championship cycle.They need to win seven of their remaining nine Tests to keep their hopes of reaching the final alive.The upcoming home series against Sri Lanka is therefore crucial, with India targeting a 2-0 sweep before travelling to New Zealand for what is expected to be a far more challenging assignment.Dhoni, meanwhile, has remained away from competitive cricket after missing the entire IPL 2026 season because of persistent injury concerns, raising fresh questions over his playing future.There are reports that the former India captain is being considered for a mentorship role with Chennai Super Kings following Stephen Fleming's departure as head coach.Having failed to qualify for the playoffs in each of the last three seasons since winning the IPL title in 2023, CSK are set for a restructuring phase. Fans flooded social media with reactions to the rare height contrast. The photo capped off a big summer for Haaland, who finished third in scoring at the 2026 FIFA World Cup and led Norway to its first-ever quarterfinal appearance before the team fell to England.Erling Haaland posted a photo with Michael Jordan this past Friday, and the internet immediately started arguing about who looked taller in the frame. The Norwegian striker, still riding the high of a standout 2026 FIFA World Cup run, kept the caption simple: "No caption needed." He let the picture do the talking instead.In the image, Haaland has his arm draped around Jordan's shoulder as both men smile for the camera. Both wore sunglasses and matching shorts, with Haaland in a black perforated polo and Hermès sandals while Jordan kept it simple in a white tee and sneakers. It's the kind of low-key, off-duty shot that usually wouldn't cause much of a stir. This one did.That's because Haaland, at 6-foot-4 to 6-foot-5, is usually the biggest presence in any room he walks into on a soccer pitch.Next to Jordan, listed at 6-foot-6, he suddenly didn't look like it.Fans on X noticed right away. One user, @BurmonSachindev, wrote: "How tall is he?? Article Title: A love that waited 7 years ended in 1 month: Army major returns home draped in Tricolour
Article Text:
Major Hamza Arif had married his Hindu engineer partner just one month prior





JAISALMER: What was meant to be the beginning of a lifetime together turned into an unimaginable tragedy for Major Hamza Arif and his young bride.After spending seven years in a committed relationship and finally convincing their families to accept their marriage, the couple had tied the knot only a month ago.Before the henna on his wife's hands had even faded, fate dealt a devastating blow.Late on Thursday night, Major Hamza Arif lost his life in a horrific road accident near Jaisalmer Military Station when the Tata Safari SUV he was driving collided with a camel and overturned several times.With his death, the dreams and hopes his wife had cherished for their new life together were shattered forever.The couple had recently begun their married life with great optimism.Major Hamza had purchased a new Tata Safari SUV, and his family in Indore had already begun preparations for a grand wedding reception planned for December, when the newlyweds were expected to visit home. Instead of returning to celebrate, the young Army officer is now making his final journey wrapped in the Indian Tricolour.Photographs from the couple's wedding have gone viral on social media, capturing moments of joy, hope and togetherness.The images have deeply moved people, highlighting the heartbreaking contrast between their recent happiness and the tragedy that followed.Major Hamza Arif is survived by his parents and three sisters.He was the only son of a middle-class Bohra Muslim family, and his untimely death has left the family devastated.According to his childhood friend Aman Shukla of Indore, Major Hamza was a native of Dhanvantri Nagar, Indore.He completed his Bachelor's degree in Electrical Engineering from Chameli Devi College in 2016.Determined to serve the nation, he cleared the selection process and joined the Indian Army in 2017.Through dedication, discipline and exceptional service, he earned three promotions within just nine years, rising to the rank of Major. He was serving at Jaisalmer Military Station at the time of the accident.The fatal crash occurred around 12:30am on Thursday night, nearly 8 kilometres from Jaisalmer city, when the SUV suddenly struck a camel on the road inside the Army area.The impact was so severe that the vehicle overturned four to five times, leaving Major Hamza critically injured.Two other officers travelling with him, Lieutenant Ayushman Gusain and Lieutenant Abhinav Rathore, also sustained injuries.All three were rushed to the Army Hospital, where doctors declared Major Hamza dead. The two injured officers continue to receive treatment.Another childhood friend, Navneet Hardia, said the tragedy has left everyone in shock because Major Hamza had only recently married his Hindu engineer partner after a seven-year relationship.The couple had faced considerable challenges in persuading their families to accept their union before finally solemnising their marriage through a court marriage just a month ago."The family had been eagerly waiting for the couple to come home in December and had already started planning a grand reception," he said. "No one could have imagined that instead of welcoming the newlyweds, they would be receiving Hamza's mortal remains wrapped in the national flag."Friends said Major Hamza's wife had looked forward to building a happy life with her husband and supporting him through his Army career. Those dreams have now been cruelly cut short. Overwhelmed with grief, she is accompanying his mortal remains to Indore for his final journey.Major Hamza had recently purchased the Tata Safari SUV involved in the accident and was driving it himself when the tragedy occurred.The accident has plunged Jaisalmer Military Station and Indore into mourning. Fellow officers, soldiers, friends and relatives have remembered Major Hamza as a dedicated Army officer, a compassionate human being and a humble individual who was deeply respected by everyone who knew him.According to family members and local representatives, Major Hamza Arif's mortal remains will be brought to Indore on Saturday, where he will be laid to rest with full military honours in accordance with the traditions of the Indian Army and the religious customs of the Bohra Muslim community.His passing has left behind not only a grieving family but also a young bride whose dreams of a lifetime together were tragically cut short just weeks after their marriage.
Article Summary: Major Hamza Arif lost his life in a horrific road accident near Jaisalmer Military Station. The Tata Safari SUV he was driving collided with a camel and overturned several times. He had only recently married his Hindu engineer partner after a seven-year relationship. The couple had recently begun their married life with great optimism. The young Army officer is now making his final journey wrapped in the Indian Tricolour.

Article Title: 500,000-year-old elephant bone tool found in England reveals advanced early human technology
Article Text:
pc: Study: Elephant-bone tool (NHMUK PV UNREG 4339) from intertidal deposits at the Boxgrove Waterhole Site

How the 500,000-year-old elephant bone tool was made



Microscopic evidence confirms the elephant bone was used as a tool



Why the Boxgrove elephant bone tool is an extraordinary discovery



What the elephant bone tool reveals about early human intelligence



Half a million years ago, people living in what is now southern England were doing far more than shaping stone into cutting tools. A newly analysed elephant bone from the famous Boxgrove archaeological site suggests they were carefully choosing, modifying and carrying specialised implements made from animal remains to improve their stone-working techniques. The discovery offers one of the clearest glimpses yet of how sophisticated Acheulean technology had become during the Middle Pleistocene. Rather than using whatever materials happened to be nearby, these hominins appear to have selected an unusually durable elephant bone, shaped it into a practical hammer and repeatedly used it to maintain finely crafted flint handaxes. According to the study published in Science Advances, titled “ The earliest elephant-bone tool from Europe: An unexpected raw material for precision knapping of Acheulean handaxes ”, this represents the earliest confirmed elephant-bone knapping hammer discovered in Europe and provides fresh evidence of long-term planning in early human technology. The find also highlights the growing cognitive and technological abilities of early humans, indicating they understood the distinct properties of different raw materials and deliberately matched them to specific tasks. Such choices reflect a level of foresight, skill and innovation rarely documented from this period of human prehistory.The object itself is a fragment of elephant cortical bone measuring just over 10 centimetres long.At first glance it might seem unremarkable, but microscopic examination revealed a sequence of deliberate modifications that separated it from ordinary animal remains.The bone was first broken while it was still fresh before large flakes were intentionally removed from its edges to create a workable shape. The pattern of fractures did not resemble damage caused by trampling, weathering or attempts to extract marrow. Instead, the scars indicated deliberate shaping that prepared the fragment for use as a handheld implement.The researchers also identified fine cut marks that appear to have been made before the bone became a tool. These marks may have resulted from removing remaining soft tissue so the fragment could be prepared for later use, although the authors note that their exact purpose cannot be confirmed.The strongest evidence came from microscopic damage spread across three areas of the bone's surface. The battered patches contained clusters of pits, grooves and fine scratches unlike those expected from natural wear.Using scanning electron microscopy and chemical analysis, the team detected numerous tiny fragments of embedded flint inside these impact marks. As per the study, the combination of pits, parallel scores and flint chips is characteristic of a bone retoucher, a soft hammer used to reshape and sharpen stone tools with greater precision than a hard stone hammer could provide.The pattern of damage also suggested repeated use. The bone was probably employed to deliver relatively light blows during the final stages of maintaining cutting edges rather than during the heavy shaping of new handaxes. The researchers estimate it may have delivered well over one hundred strikes across multiple episodes of tool maintenance before being discarded or left behind.Boxgrove in West Sussex has long been recognised as one of Europe's richest Lower Palaeolithic sites, preserving evidence from roughly 480,000 years ago. Excavations have uncovered hundreds of carefully made handaxes, butchered animal remains, rare human fossils and numerous bone and antler implements associated with flint working.According to the paper, the elephant bone hammer fits into a much broader technological toolkit. Early humans at Boxgrove were already using different kinds of hammers for different stages of tool production. Hard stone hammers helped rough out handaxes, while softer antler and bone tools allowed finer thinning, sharpening and reshaping. The elephant bone appears to have been selected for these more delicate finishing tasks because of its thick, durable outer layer.The researchers also point out that elephant bones are exceptionally rare at Boxgrove, making the choice of raw material especially significant. The bone was probably collected elsewhere, shaped before arriving at the site and transported for repeated use, suggesting that valuable tools were curated rather than simply made and discarded where they were found.The find adds another piece to a growing picture of Middle Pleistocene hominins as flexible and thoughtful toolmakers rather than simple stone knappers. Producing the refined Boxgrove handaxes required careful selection of raw materials, the use of different hammer types for different stages of manufacture and the ability to plan. They argue that the elephant-bone tool demonstrates deliberate resource selection, repeated maintenance of equipment and an adaptable technological approach suited to changing environments. Such behaviour, the researchers suggest, helped these populations expand into cooler parts of Europe and cope with increasingly varied landscapes.
Article Summary: Microscopic evidence confirms the elephant bone was used as a tool. Discovery offers one of the clearest glimpses yet of how sophisticated Acheulean technology had become during the Middle Pleistocene. Early humans at Boxgrove were already using different kinds of hammers for different stages of tool production.

Article Title: Scientists discover ancient silk production in Uzbekistan nearly 2,000 years before the Silk Road
Article Text:
image AI generated

Ancient silkworm cocoons found at Bronze Age Sapalli Tepe in Uzbekistan



Ancient mulberry trees and silkworm cocoons provide evidence of early silk production



Sapalli Tepe discovery suggests sericulture began long before the Silk Road



How domesticated silkworms may have reached Central Asia before the Silk Road



For generations, the history of silk has been told in a fairly straightforward way. Domesticated silkworms emerged in ancient China, silk travelled westward once the Silk Road developed, and the knowledge required to raise silkworms followed the same route. That sequence has shaped both archaeological research and popular history for decades. The story may be far older and rather less linear. Evidence recovered from Bronze Age settlements in present-day Uzbekistan suggests that people in southern Central Asia were already cultivating mulberry trees and raising domesticated silkworms around 2000 BCE. If the findings withstand further scrutiny, they would shift the accepted timeline for organised sericulture in the region by almost two millenniaThe research centres on Sapalli Tepe, a Bronze Age settlement in southern Uzbekistan belonging to the Oxus or Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex. During excavations, archaeologists recovered three ancient silkworm cocoons alongside plant remains preserved in archaeological deposits.According to the new study published in Science Advances, titled “ Silkworm cultivation predating the Silk Road in southern Central Asia (2000 BCE) ”, the cocoons were directly dated to between 1940 and 1765 BCE. Laboratory analyses, including protein fingerprinting, identified them as belonging to Bombyx mori, the domesticated mulberry silkworm, rather than unrelated silk-producing insects.The authors note that the cocoons resemble wild silkworms in appearance, yet their protein signatures align with domesticated Bombyx mori. That combination raises the possibility that these insects represent an early stage in the history of domesticated silkworm populations rather than modern forms.The cocoons were not the only evidence pointing towards organised silk production. More than 1,200 fragments of ancient wood charcoal were analysed from three Bronze Age sites. Among them were charcoal remains identified as Morus (mulberry), the essential food source for domesticated silkworms. The study states that these are the earliest known archaeological remains of mulberry trees from Central Asia.The team also found that mulberry charcoal appeared at all three settlements and became increasingly common through time. Other cultivated plants, including grapes, figs, citrus, barley, wheat, millets and flax, were also identified, suggesting these communities managed a diverse agricultural landscape rather than relying on a limited range of crops.As per the study, the combination of domesticated silkworm cocoons and mulberry remains provides strong evidence that silkworm rearing was taking place locally instead of silk simply arriving through exchange.Traditional historical accounts place the spread of Chinese sericulture into Central Asia during or after the Han Dynasty, when Silk Road trade expanded from the late second century BCE.The new findings challenge that chronology. The discoveries at Sapalli Tepe indicate that communities in southern Central Asia were already practising mulberry-based sericulture roughly 2,000 years before the commonly accepted beginning of Silk Road exchanges.This evidence places silk production alongside other examples of prehistoric movement across Eurasia, including crops, livestock and horticultural knowledge that travelled between East, Central and South Asia during the third and second millennia BCE.The researchers also refer to a previously excavated silk-like textile fragment from Sapalli Tepe, together with numerous textile-making tools recovered from Bronze Age settlements in the region. While these objects alone cannot prove local silk manufacture, they fit the wider archaeological picture emerging from the new analyses.The archaeological evidence currently represents a single well-documented case outside eastern China, making it difficult to identify the exact route by which domesticated silkworms and mulberry cultivation reached Central Asia.One possibility proposed in the paper is movement along the southern slopes of the Himalayas, supported by comparisons with archaeological evidence for mulberry remains and long-standing cultural connections between the Oxus civilisation and the Indus region. At the same time, the researchers emphasise that a northern route cannot yet be ruled out and that additional discoveries will be needed before any dispersal pathway can be confirmed.Reportedly, the evidence from Sapalli Tepe establishes the earliest documented occurrence of mulberry-Bombyx sericulture outside ancient China. Rather than presenting silk production as an innovation that spread only after the Silk Road emerged.
Article Summary: Ancient mulberry trees and silkworm cocoons provide evidence of early silk production. Discovery at Sapalli Tepe suggests sericulture began long before the Silk Road. If the findings withstand further scrutiny, they would shift the accepted timeline for organised sericulture in the region by almost two millennia.

Article Title: “Three-against-one situation”: El Rubius opens up on being “targeted” in MrBeast’s viral $1M challenge
Article Text:
El Rubius reacted honestly after his elimination from MrBeast’s $1 million challenge, calling it “unfair” and claiming he was targeted in a three-against-one situation. Despite his frustration, he thanked fans and gave away his $50,000 winnings. His response felt real and balanced, especially after MrBeast’s team later sent him a cake, softening the moment.

El Rubius reflects on a tough and “unfair” exit







El Rubius did not just walk away from MrBeast’s $1 million streamer challenge. He opened up. Soon after his elimination, the Spanish creator shared a raw reaction with fans, giving them a closer look at what the experience felt like from inside the game. It was not polished or carefully framed. It felt real, and that is exactly why it caught attention so quickly.The clip and his response have since fueled conversations across the streaming space. Some viewers believe intense competitions like this naturally lead to uneven situations. Others feel Rubius may have had a point about being singled out. Either way, his words have added a human layer to a challenge that many only saw as entertainment.Speaking through an Instagram Story, Rubius did not hide his frustration, but he also made sure to thank his supporters. He said, "Guys, I just got knocked out of the game. It was a bit of an unfair elimination, but hey, at least I managed to walk away with $50,000 for you all, which I’ve already distributed. It went to the mods, the subs, and the non-subs alike."He further added, "I’m happy, of course, though admittedly, it was incredibly tough.I wasn't really a fan of the challenge itself, either. But then again... it was basically a three-against-one situation the entire time. I mean, they were targeting me specifically the whole way through. I kept trying to go after RaKai, but, well, he actually just got eliminated in the end. So, at least justice was served for Abraham. Abraham, if you’re watching this, we were all rooting for you, and standing right there with you."His message carried mixed emotions. There was disappointment, yes, but also pride in how he handled things. Giving away his $50,000 winnings to his community stood out as a gesture that meant more than the result itself.He continued with another honest note, saying, "And in the end, karma finally caught up with that little punk. Sorry, I’m being a bit toxic right now, but let's just hope the MrBeast team doesn't see this! Guys, thank you all so much. Seriously, thank you for all the support and for just being there."He added, "Every time I asked for something in the chat or whatever it was, you guys were right there. You’re incredible. I’m a little disappointed in myself, personally, mostly for not performing better, but hey, I gave it my all, and we still walked away with $50,000, so we’ve got to look on the bright side. All right, guys, big hugs to all my brothers out there!"Interestingly, the story did not end with frustration. Later that day, Rubius revealed that MrBeast’s team had sent him a cake after his exit. It was a small gesture, but it shifted the mood. It showed that even in a high-pressure challenge, there is still room for respect.In the end, Rubius’ reaction felt honest and grounded. That is what stayed with people.
Article Summary: El Rubius was eliminated from MrBeast's $1 million streamer challenge. He called it "unfair" and said he was targeted in a three-against-one situation. Despite his frustration, he thanked fans and gave away his $50,000 winnings.
